strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: predicting factual QA failures before generating an answer. The lightweight probe offers a practical way to use question representations without fine-tuning the underlying LLM. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b04/review-experiment-2ijbjip2/call-ee4ab33c97b44d019f6130b5b00f5794/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The experimental coverage is substantial: four primary LLMs, three QA datasets, and supplementary HotpotQA and Gemma experiments. Table 1 shows competitive or better performance against several relevant baselines, including full fine-tuning and LoRA. Representation-layer and token-selection ablations help substantiate the design.

The transfer results are promising independently of the proposed explanation. For example, LLaMA2-to-LLaMA3 transfer on PopQA improves from 0.443 to 0.842 AUC with adaptation. The question-aligned training ablation provides additional evidence that the training procedure matters.

The simple architecture, code link, dataset filtering details, deterministic decoding, and reported optimization settings support reproducibility. Table 2 also provides useful efficiency measurements and explicitly acknowledges representation-extraction costs.
weaknesses: The central inference about shared conditional distributions is not established. Section 4.2 argues that comparable pooled-model and individual-model performance verifies little concept shift. However, equal AUC does not imply equal P(y|X), and a pooled nonlinear classifier can exploit domain-specific representation regions to implement different predictors. Agreement between fitted models and supervised t-SNE visualizations do not resolve this ambiguity. The empirical transfer results support the method more convincingly than this claimed explanation.

The label-quality estimate has an unsupported premise. Section 3.2, footnote 4 assumes that all positive, non-factual labels are correct and audits only 240 negative examples. Failure to contain a gold-answer substring can nevertheless arise from a valid paraphrase or an unlisted alias. Consequently, the stated 97% label accuracy is not established. Both classes need a stratified manual audit, with performance checked against the corrected labels.

The label-free transfer evaluation is insufficiently specified. Appendix C.2 explains checkpoint selection for single-LLM probes but does not clearly state how cross-LLM checkpoints are selected without target labels. Figures 7 and 13 track target-test AUC over training, and kernel preference is justified using these curves. This does not demonstrate leakage, but a reproducible selection rule independent of target labels is essential to substantiate the transfer claim.

The controls do not adequately distinguish model-specific knowledge prediction from general question difficulty. Useful comparisons include a generic question-embedding classifier and the source model's probe evaluated against target-model outcomes while retaining source representations. Directly feeding target activations into an unadapted source probe is a weak transfer baseline because representation coordinates differ. Evaluating questions on which source and target correctness disagree would strengthen the interpretation considerably.

Statistical and practical reliability remain underexplored. Results lack uncertainty estimates or repeated runs, despite some small differences and only 1,244 NQ questions before splitting. AUC establishes ranking performance, but does not validate the probability interpretation or deployment thresholds. Calibration and risk–coverage evaluation would be more informative than the uncontrolled demo ratings.

The empirical contribution makes this close to Findings, but the unresolved labeling and transfer-selection issues prevent a clear soundness and reproducibility endorsement. The assessment is driven by these evidential gaps, rather than the method's modest architectural novelty.
